lines.text: is it not true that what we experience at such times is usually
soon forgotten? Do we not normally become once more
quickly caught up in life with its claims, its this-worldly
values and purposes, the pressing responsibilities of the day
and moment? So that, in fine, this world is for us equated
with reality? But is it not possible that we viewed reality
more deeply and fully in those moments of failure in which
all the turmoil and striving of this world struck us as alien
and, in essence, of questionable value?
"The most frightening dream is accompanied by a secret
feeling that it all means nothing, howsoever we sweat with
fear. A loving smile shines gently upon our tears. But I
would like to think that it must always be so."1
Yes, in fact it should always be so; we should always be
prepared to see the realities of this world and our life within
them as appearance only, in which genuine reality does not
inhere—or which can become real only through ourselves,
when we ourselves are living in the power of a higher, more
genuine reality as a result of which we can transform our
life in the world. For of course the Christian faith and
discipleship to Jesus is not a mere matter of resignation, it is
not merely a feeling of homelessness in the world, it is not
simply something negative. Rather it is just the consciousness
of living in the fullness of a power which streams from super-
natural, ultimate reality. But to receive this power demands
the readiness to adopt an attitude of inner detachment from
the world, so that we move in it as though we did not belong
to it, are active within it, rejoice or mourn in it as though
we did not do so. In the last resort this means that we should
be detached from ourselves, from that restless life which we
know to be active in our wishes and plans, our work and
our enjoyment. What is required from us is the confession
that we are not those who see, but are blind.
"For judgment I came into this world, that those who do
not see may see and that those who see may become blind."
This means that following Jesus requires from us a resigna-
